Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 93, verse 1:

Surat al-Duha

It is a Meccan surah, and its verses number eleven without any disagreement. When, in what precedes it, Allah, glorified is He, mentioned, ﴿And the most pious will be spared it﴾, and the master of the most pious was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He followed that with a mention of His blessings, mighty and majestic is He, upon him (ﷺ). The Imam (al-Razi) said: When the first surah was the surah of Abu Bakr (radiyallahu anhu) and this one is the surah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), He, majestic and exalted is He, followed one with the other and did not place an intermediary between them, so that it would be known that there is no intermediary between His Messenger (ﷺ) and the Siddiq (radiyallahu anhu). The placing of the surah of the Siddiq before the surah of the Messenger, peace be upon him, does not indicate that he is superior to him (ﷺ). Do you not see that He, exalted is He, first swore by something of His creation, then swore by Himself, mighty and majestic is He, in a number of places, among them the preceding surah, as you know? Servants may go before masters, and many sunnahs are commanded to be placed before the obligatory acts of worship. The blossom is not harmed by being later than its branches, nor the spear by its being at the ends of its shaft. Then, what he mentioned is the flower of spring, which does not bear rubbing, as is not hidden.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿By the morning brightness﴾. The discussion of it has already passed. The intended meaning here is the time of the sun's rising that follows the time of its appearance to the observers, not its light and its elevation, because that is more fitting to what follows. Its being singled out for an oath is because it is the youth of the day, and its state is one of strength, not close to its opposite. For this reason it is counted as a daily honour for the sun and a good fortune. Also, according to what they say, it is the hour in which Allah, exalted is He, spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, and in which the sorcerers were cast down prostrating, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the people be gathered at morning brightness﴾. Thus there is a suitability to what is sworn about, namely that He, exalted is He, did not leave the Prophet (ﷺ), and His gentle kindness and His speaking, glorified is He, did not part from him. It has been said: the intended meaning is the daytime, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when Our punishment comes to them in the morning brightness﴾. This was objected to on the basis of a distinction: there it stands in contrast to the night-raid (bayat), which is the night in general, whereas here it stands in contrast to the night, restricted in meaning by the intensifying of its darkness; so the fitting interpretation is the time of its rising and the strength of its light. It was answered by denying that the restriction indicates intensification, and you will hear, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, what is in that. Whichever it is, the apparent meaning is that the intended is the genus, that is: and the genus of morning brightness.

[Page 154]

"By the night when it becomes still" (﴿واللَّيْلِ إذا سَجى﴾). That is, and by the species of night, when it becomes still. Its people have settled down. The root is from *sajā*, which, as many have said, means stillness in general. The attribution is figurative, or it involves an elided element (*taqdīr al-muḍāf*), as has been said. Similar to this is what is reported from Qatadah, meaning that people and sounds become quiet during it. This usually happens between its two ends, or after a period has passed from its beginning. Or its darkness becomes settled, from the phrase *sajā al-baḥr*, "the sea became calm, its waves stilled." Al-A'sha said:

*"What is our fault that the sea of the son of your paternal uncle surged, while your sea is still and does not conceal the seaweed?"*

It has been said that *al-sajw*, in this sense, originally means the stilling of the waves, and then it became general. What is meant by the stillness of its darkness is that it does not change through intensifying or descending, that is, in what is sensed and apparent. This is the case when it is fully complete in perception, with the sun reaching the level of the foot and its vicinity and what is near it. Ibn al-A'rabi explicitly took intensification into account when he said: "*Sajā al-layl*: its darkness intensified." Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "That is, when it comes and covers everything." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported through al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas the explanation of *sajā* as *aqbala* ("came"), without mention of covering. Both of them, along with Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, also reported from him that he said: "*Sajā* means it went away." Both explanations contradict the well-known meaning. It is common to say: "a night that is still (*sākin*) or calm (*sāj*)" for a night in which there is no wind. Describing it with this, I mean stillness, has been said to be literal, as when one says: "a night with no wind." It is not said that the one who is still is in reality the wind, because stillness in the literal sense is impossible for it, since it is moving air. Moreover, they say this of a night with no wind, not of one whose wind has become still. The correct position is that stillness, in both of its senses, namely the absence of movement in something that is capable of movement, or the presence of two bodies in one space, does not apply to the night, because it is a specific period of time. Nonetheless, since the stillness of the air is like its absence in common usage, due to lack of perception, or because it includes the absence of wind (not of air), it is said: "a calm and still night." The night is described literally, that is, there is no attribution to something unsuitable. It is possible to take stillness in this sense as a customary literal meaning. It has also been permitted to interpret what is in the verse in terms of this common meaning. Perhaps the restriction to this is because a night without wind is further from calamities. Some jurists have mentioned that a strong wind at night is one of the excuses for not attending congregational prayer.

It is reported from Qatadah and Muqatil that what is meant by "the forenoon" (*al-ḍuḥā*) is the forenoon in which God spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, and by "the night" the Night of the Ascension (*Laylat al-Mi'rāj*).

Some people explained "the forenoon" as the face of the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and "the night" as his hair, peace be upon him, as the Imam mentioned, and he said: "There is nothing unlikely about it." But this is, as you see, far-fetched. Similar to it is what has been said: "the forenoon" refers to the male members of the Prophet's household, peace be upon him, and "the night" to their female members. The Imam said: "It is possible to say: the forenoon is his prophethood, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and the night is the period in which revelation was withheld, because in the time of its descent there was companionship, and in the time of its withholding there was loneliness. Or the forenoon is the light of His knowledge, exalted is He, by which He knows what is hidden of the unseen, and the night is His pardon, exalted is He, by which all faults are covered. Or the forenoon is the rising of Islam after it had been strange, and the night indicates that it will return to being strange. Or the forenoon is perfection of intellect, and the night is the state of death. Or the forenoon is his openness, peace be upon him, in which the creation sees no fault, and the night is his secret, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, which the knower of the unseen does not find faulty." End of quotation. It should not be overlooked that this is not part of the tafsir at all, and the domain of ta'wil (esoteric interpretation) and isharah (allusive interpretation) includes much more than this.

The placement of "the forenoon" before "the night," based on what we said at the beginning, is to honour its nobility, because in it the increase of light appears, and light has an intrinsic nobility over darkness, either because it is existential, or because of the abundance of its benefits, or because of its affinity with the world of the angels, for they are luminous. The placement of "the night" in the preceding surah is because in it there is darkness, which, being an absence, is the origin of the light that comes into being through the removal of it by occurring causes. It has also been said that its placement there is because the surah concerns Abu Bakr, and he was preceded by disbelief, while the placement of "the forenoon" here is because the surah concerns the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, and he was not preceded by that.

As for God's specifying these two times with an oath, it has been said that by their states He, glorified is He, indicates what happened to him, peace be upon him, and confirms the negation of what was imagined about him, exalted and majestic is He. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: time is one hour, and an hour is an hour of night and an hour of day. Then at times the hours of night increase and the hours of day decrease, and at other times the reverse. Neither the increase is due to desire, nor the decrease due to aversion. Rather, each is for a wisdom. Likewise the matter of revelation: at one time it is a sending down, and at another a withholding. Neither the sending down was out of desire, nor the withholding out of aversion, but each is for a wisdom. It has also been said that by their states He, glorified and exalted is He, consoles His beloved, peace be upon him, as if He, glorified is He, says: Look at these two neighbours, neither of which is safe from the other. Rather, the night overcomes at times and the day at others. So how do you expect to be safe from the creation? The two statements are based on the premise that what is meant by "the forenoon" is [Page 155] the entire day, and by "the night when it becomes still" the entire night. The specification of the forenoon, as you heard at first, is for what you heard. The specification of the night, based on the premise that what is meant is the time when darkness intensifies, has been said to be because it is the time when the lover is alone with the beloved, and safe from every informer and watcher. Al-Tibi, may God purify his resting place, said concerning this: God, exalted is He, swore to him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, by two times in which are his prayers, peace be upon him, which were made the coolness of his eye and the cause of his greater nearness and intimacy. As for the forenoon, it is because of what al-Daraqutni related in *al-Mujtabā* from Ibn Abbas, traced back to the Prophet: "The sacrifice (*al-naḥr*) was prescribed for me and not prescribed for you, and I was commanded to pray the forenoon prayer and you were not commanded to do so."

As for the night, it is because of God's saying: ﴿And during part of the night, pray with it as an additional prayer for you﴾, to humble His enemies and to refute them in their claim of His abandonment and forsaking of him. It is as if it were said: By the right of your nearness to Us and your station with Us, We have chosen you, and We have not forsaken you or become displeased with you. This is like His saying:

*"And your front teeth, indeed they are like the bright buds of flowers."*

This is something the people of spiritual tastes find pleasing. It is possible that the oath by the night, according to what was reported from Qatadah, is also of this kind, as is the oath by both of them on some of the aspects previously mentioned, as is not hidden. And on the basis that what is meant by "the forenoon" is the known time of the day, and by "the night" all of it, it has been said: the distinction is to indicate that one hour of the day equals the whole night, just as the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, equals all the prophets, peace be upon them. It is also to indicate, since the day is the time of joy and the night the time of loneliness and grief, that the cares and sorrows of this world last longer than its joys.

It has been reported that "when God created the Throne, a cloud shaded over its left side and called out: 'What shall I rain?' It was commanded to rain down sorrows and griefs, and it rained for a hundred years. Then it cleared, and it was commanded again in the same way, and so on until three hundred years had been completed. Then a white cloud shaded over the right side of the Throne and called out: 'What shall I rain?' It was commanded to rain down joy for an hour." Therefore you see sorrows and griefs lasting longer than pleasures in this world. God, exalted is He, knows best the soundness of the report, and others have said other than this.

And His saying, ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you﴾, etc. This is the answer to the oath. *Wadda'a* comes from *tawdi'* (farewell). Originally it derives from *da'ah* (ease, comfort): you pray for the traveler that God removes from him the hardship of travel and grants him ease and comfort of life, just as *taslim* (greeting) is a prayer for his safety. Then it became the common expression for seeing off a traveler and for leaving, and then it was used for leaving in general, and it is interpreted in this sense here. That is: "Your Lord has not left you." In *al-Bahr* and *al-Kashshaf* it is said: *tawdi'* is an intensified form of *wad'*, meaning "leaving," because whoever bids you farewell as he departs has gone to great lengths in leaving you. It has been said: according to this, the negated thing would be the intensified leaving, not the leaving itself, while the apparent sense is the negation of that (the leaving itself). Therefore one must say: it negated that only because it is what occurred in the speech of the polytheists, which occasioned the revelation of the verse; or the intensification returns to the negation, so the meaning is intensification in the negation, not the negation of intensification. They mentioned a parallel to these two views in His saying, ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾, so reflect.

It has also been said: the meaning is "He did not cut you off in the manner of one who bids farewell." *Tawdi'* is then a metaphor, a *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a derived metaphor), for leaving, and in it there is such gentleness and honor as is not hidden. For a farewell occurs only between loved ones, and one whose parting is painful, as al-Mutanabbi said:

*A remnant of a soul that bade farewell on the day they bade farewell,*
*so I did not know which of the departing ones I should escort.*

The true meaning of the common farewell is not conceivable here. It was objected that on this view it would not be a refutation of what the polytheists said, for they did not say "his Lord bade him farewell" in this sense. How could they, when they were far from believing that he, upon him be blessings and peace, held the station he holds with his Lord, glorified is He? It was answered: it is possible that "his Lord bade him farewell" indicates that meaning, but the polytheists—may God fight them—said it as mockery and derision, and when He answered them, He intended what the word implies in its true sense.

It has also been said: the leaving in their speech is absolute, and the apparent state of them is that they did not intend the quiddity (essence) as such, nor its realization in some form that does not harm the noble station of him, upon him be blessings and peace; rather they intended the quiddity as realized in some form that harms that station. Since the aim was to comfort him, upon him be blessings and peace, and to remove his loneliness, upon him be blessings and peace, something was brought that contains the negation of what they claimed in the most emphatic manner, as if it were said: "This kind of leaving, which does not harm your station, was not even a fraction of the leaving they claimed, which harms your mighty station." But in my view, the apparent meaning is that this statement, in whatever sense it was made, was issued as mockery, if the word "Lord" refers to God, mighty and majestic, and the speaker was one of the polytheists, as is not hidden to the one who reflects.

 Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, his son Hisham, Abu Haywah, Abu Bahriyyah and Ibn Abi Ablah read: *ma wada'aka* (without the doubling), and according to Ibn Jinni this is the reading of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. It is construed as *wada'a* being a lightened form of *wadda'a*, with the same meaning. In al-Qamus: "*wada'ahu* is like *wada'ahu* (to place), and *wadda'a* has the same meaning." It has been said: it is not a lightened form, but a verb in its own right, meaning "to leave." This would contradict the grammarians' claim that the Arabs made the past tense of *yada'u* and *yadhar* (to leave), their verbal noun, active participle and passive participle obsolete, and used *yatruku* (to leave) instead. In *al-Maghrib* it is said that the grammarians claimed the Arabs made that obsolete, yet the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was the most eloquent of them, and he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Let people cease from abandoning the congregations."

He recited: *ma wada'aka*. Abu al-Aswad said:

*I wish I knew about my friend what it is that*
*overcame him in love, so that he left him.*

A similar line is that of another:

*And then we left the family of Amr and Amir*
*as prey for the tips of the straight, dark spears.*

This is also evidence that *wada'a* is used in the sense of *taraka* (to leave), with two objects, so do not be heedless.

In a hadith: "Leave the Turks as long as they leave you, and leave the Abyssinians as long as they leave you."

In *al-Mustawfa* it is said that all of this has come in the speech of the Arabs, and there is no weight to the speech of the grammarians. When the river of God comes, the river of Ma'qil dries up. Yes, its occurrence is rare. Al-Tibi, after mentioning its occurrence in verse and prose, said: What made this reading good is the agreement between the two words—meaning this and what follows it—as in the hadith of the Turks and the Abyssinians; for the echoing of the final part to the first part and the artistic figure of *tarsi'* (rhyming parallelism) have compensated for it. It has also been said: the speakers only said "his Lord has left him" with the lightened form, and so this was revealed. The beauty of the reading then lies in intending *mushakalah* (matching) with what they said, and they spoke with an unfamiliar word out of ill-omen (*tiyarah*): the unfamiliar word was among those words regarded as inauspicious, a bad omen. Or, when they intended mockery, the use of the word was fitting; and they have said: unfamiliar words and the like are fitting in satire, so it is not far-fetched that it is the same in mockery. The truth is that, once its occurrence is established, it needs no strained justification to make it good. The apparent meaning is that the Lord refers to God, mighty and majestic. In expressing Him by the title of Lordship and attributing it to the pronoun of him, upon him be blessings and peace, there is gentleness that is not hidden. It is as if it were said: "He who has taken charge of your welfare and who conveys to you, step by step, your perfection that befits you, has not forsaken you."

﴿Nor has He detested you﴾: that is, He has not hated you. The object was omitted so that he, upon him be blessings and peace, would not be confronted with the attribution of detestation to him, even though it occurs in a negated statement, out of gentleness toward him, may God bless him and grant him peace, and out of compassion for him, upon him be blessings and peace. Or it is to negate its occurrence from Him, mighty and majestic, in relation to him, may God bless him and grant him peace, and to any of his companions and whoever loves him, may God bless him and grant him peace, until the Day of Resurrection. Or it is because the object was already mentioned earlier, together with the consideration of rhyme (*fawasil*). The well-known dialect of the present tense of *qala* (to detest) is *yaqli*, like *yarmi* (to throw); the Tayy tribe say *yaqla* with a fatha on the ʿayn, like *yarda*. The explanation of *qila* as hatred is widespread. In al-Qamus, from the waw-root: *qala Zaydan qilan* and *qalahu* (he hated him), and from the ya-root: *qalahu*, like *rama-hu*, and "he was pleased with him (*radiya*) with *qila*," and *qalahu maqilah*: he hated him and disliked him to the utmost extent of dislike, so he left him; or *qalahu* in abandonment and *qaliyahu* in hatred. In al-Raghib's *Mufradat*: *qila* is intense hatred; one says *qalahu yaqluhu* and *yaqlihi*. Whoever takes it from the waw-root takes it from *quluww*, that is, throwing, from their saying: "The she-camel threw her rider (*qalat*) with a throw (*qalwan*), and I threw with the pebble (*qallah*)," so the one who is thrown (*maqlu*) is the one whom the heart casts out from its hatred, so it does not accept him. And whoever takes it from the ya-root takes it from *qalaytu al-busr wa al-sawiq ʿala al-miqlah* (I fried the unripe dates and the barley-meal on the frying-pan), and the end. Between the two there is a difference that is not hidden.

Taking intense hatred as the sense, the apparent view is that this is in the verse only because it is what occurred in their speech. The commentators said: Gabriel, upon him be peace, delayed to come to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, so the polytheists said: "His Lord has detested him and bade him farewell," and God revealed that.

Al-Hakim transmitted from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "When ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ and what follows was revealed, it was said to the wife of Abu Lahab, Umm Jamil: 'Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, has satirized you.' She came to him, upon him be blessings and peace, while he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was sitting among the company, and she said: 'O Muhammad, why do you satirize me?' He said: 'By God, I did not satirize you; it is God, mighty and majestic, who satirized you.' She said: 'Have you seen me carrying firewood, or with a rope of palm-fiber around my neck?' Then she departed. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, remained without revelation descending upon him. She came to him and said: 'I see that your companion has only bidden you farewell and detested you.' Then God revealed that."

At-Tirmidhi transmitted it as authentic, and Ibn Abi Hatim, and the wording is his, from Jundub al-Bajali, who said: "The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was struck by a stone on his finger, and he said: 'You are only a finger that bled, and in the way of God you have suffered what you have suffered.' Then he remained for two nights or three without rising, and a woman said to him: 'I see that your devil has only left you.'"

And in another narration also by at-Tirmidhi, Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and a group, with the wording: "The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, fell ill, and he did not rise for two nights or three, so God revealed: ﴿By the morning brightness﴾, ﴿and by the night when it is still﴾, ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you nor has He detested you﴾."

It does not include the story of the woman, nor the stone and the verse of *rijz* (poetic meter), and that does not discredit its authenticity.

A group of commentators said: "The Jews asked him, upon him be blessings and peace, about the People of the Cave, about the Spirit, and about the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'I will inform you tomorrow,' and he did not make the exception (*istithna'*, saying 'God willing'). Revelation was withheld from him, so the polytheists said what they said, and then this was revealed."

It has also been said: "Uthman gave him, upon him be blessings and peace, a cluster of grapes, and it was said: a palm-bunch of dates. A beggar came and he gave it to him. Then Uthman bought it back for a dirham and presented it to him a second time, then the beggar returned and it was given to him, and so three times. He, upon him be blessings and peace, said, gently and not angrily: 'Are you a beggar, O so-and-so, or a merchant?' Then revelation was delayed for days, and he felt lonely, so this was revealed." Perhaps they also said what they said.

Ibn Abi Shaybah in his *Musnad*, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from the hadith of Khawlah, who used to serve the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: "A puppy entered under the bed of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and died, and we did not notice it. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, remained four days without revelation descending upon him. He said: 'O Khawlah, what has happened in the house of the Messenger of God, upon him be blessings and peace? Gabriel does not come to me!' I said: 'O Prophet of God, no day has come upon us better than today.' He took his cloak, put it on and went out. I said to myself: 'If only I prepared the house and swept it.' I swept under the bed with the broom, and suddenly there was something heavy. I kept at it until the puppy appeared to me dead. I took it with my hand and threw it behind the house. Then the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, came, his beard trembling, and when revelation descended upon him he would be seized by trembling. He said: 'O Khawlah, wrap me up!' Then God revealed: ﴿By the morning brightness﴾, ﴿and by the night﴾ up to His saying: ﴿so that you will be well pleased﴾."

This narration indicates that the interruption lasted four days.

From Ibn Jurayj: it was twelve days. From al-Kalbi: fifteen days; it has also been said: about ten days. From Ibn ʿAbbas: twenty-five days. From al-Suddi and Muqatil: forty days. You know that such matters vary in their knowledge of their beginning, and it is hardly known with certainty except from him, upon him be blessings and peace. And God knows best.

In some narrations there is evidence that the one who said this was the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace.

From al-Hasan, who said: "Revelation was delayed to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he said to Khadijah: 'My Lord has bidden me farewell and detested me.'" He complained to her, and she said: "Never! By Him who sent you with the truth, God did not begin with you this honor except that He, glorified is He, wishes to complete it for you." Then this was revealed.

The commentary raises an objection to this report: it is not fitting for the Messenger ﷺ to think that Allah, exalted is He, had bid him farewell and come to dislike him. This would amount to nothing other than a kind of dismissal, and dismissing a Prophet from prophethood is not permitted by Allah's wisdom, glorified and exalted is He. The Prophet (ﷺ) knows this better, and he also knows that the delay of revelation (wahy, divine revelation) and its opposite each carry some benefit and wisdom. The answer given is that, if it is authentically established, his intention (ﷺ) in saying this was to test her, to know the extent of her knowledge, or to let the people know that. He said what he said (ﷺ) in some form of interpretation, such as that he meant: "My Lord has bid me farewell and disliked me," according to the claim of the polytheists, or that his Lord's treatment of him through the delay of revelation resembles the treatment of one who bids farewell and one who dislikes. You know that this report is anomalous (shadhdh), not relied upon, and not heeded, so there is no need to exhaust the mind in interpreting it.

[Page 158]

Similar to it is what indicates that the one who said that was Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Urwah, who said: Jibril (peace be upon him) delayed coming to the Prophet (ﷺ), so he grieved greatly. Khadijah said: "I see that your Lord has disliked you, given what I see of your grief." Then there was revealed: ﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night...﴾ to its end.

As for the view that she (may Allah be pleased with her) meant that this grief should only come from your Lord's disliking you, and far be it that He should dislike you, this grief is far from it, to the utmost degree of distance. What the majority rely upon, and what the reports authentically establish, is that the one who said it was the polytheists, and that what grieved him (peace be upon him) was, by the requirement of human nature, their expression and the absence of seeing Jibril (peace be upon him), along with his great love for him.

In some reports it is related that he (ﷺ) said to Jibril (peace be upon him): "You did not come to me until I longed for you." Jibril (peace be upon him) said: "I was more longing for you, but I am a servant who is commanded," and he recited: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾

In another narration, he (peace be upon him) reproached him for both of these, and said: "Do you not know that we do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture?"

The narrator of this report also relates that the reason for the delay of revelation was the presence of a puppy in the house of the Prophet (peace be upon him). The reports on this differ. Some have allowed that the delay was due to a convergence of causes. Then some have claimed, based on some of the earlier reports, that it is permissible for "your Lord" in ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you﴾ to refer to something other than what follows "your companion," and that what is meant by it is Jibril (peace be upon him). And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 93, verse 4:

Since what preceded contained the denial of abandonment and of hatred, namely that He, Mighty and Majestic is He, does not cease to continue His revelation and honour to him, upon him be prayers and peace, in this world, the Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, was given good news that what he will be given in the Hereafter is greater and more magnificent than that. So it was said: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾, because it is everlasting, pure and free of impurities absolutely, whereas this world is transient and mixed with harms. Although the nobility of prophethood that he, upon him be prayers and peace, was given is something that no nobility can equal and no excellence can approach, it is not free in this world from some obstacles that impair the implementation of the rulings. Moreover, what has been prepared for him, upon him be prayers and peace, in the Hereafter includes precedence and superiority over all the Prophets and Messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, on the Day of Assembly, the Day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds; his community being witnesses over all other nations; the raising of the ranks of the believers and the elevation of their stations through his intercession, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace; and other noble honours that words cannot encompass and allusions fall short of. These are, as stated in al-Irshad, like some beginnings in relation to the goals. As for the specificity that the lam implies, it was said to be relative (idafi), meaning that he, upon him be prayers and peace, is specifically granted the superiority of the Hereafter over those who harmed him and mocked the delay of revelation to him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. There is no objection to its being general to all the successful, since it is known necessarily that the good prepared for him, upon him be prayers and peace, is better than what is prepared for anyone else absolutely. It suffices for this that the Praised Station (al-maqam al-mahmud) is specific to him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. Also, the specificity of the lam is not restrictive (qasri), as established in its proper place. Taking al-akhirah to mean the Hereafter as opposed to this world, and al-ula to mean the first abode, which is this world, is the apparent interpretation transmitted from Abu Ishaq and others.

Ibn 'Atiyya and a group said:

It is possible that by them is meant the end of his affair, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, and its beginning. So the lam in them is for definiteness (al-'ahd) or a substitute for the genitive noun that follows; that is: the end of your affair is better than its beginning, as it continues to increase in strength and ascend in elevation. In some elevated (marfu') narrations there is what is more apparent for the first (interpretation).

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said: "What is to be opened for my community after me was shown to me, and it pleased me." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾.

Then, the connection of the verse with what precedes in the manner you have heard is what many of the eminent scholars chose. It is also permissible to say about it: when there was revealed ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He hated you﴾, he, upon him be prayers and peace, received a great honour thereby, so it is as if he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, regarded that as great, so it was said to him: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾, meaning that this honour, although great, what is for you with Allah the Exalted in the Hereafter is better and greater.

It is also permissible that the meaning is that the cessation of revelation cannot be for what they imagine, because it would be dismissal from prophethood, which is impossible in wisdom. Rather, at most, it could be because he has come to be without need of the message, and that is a sign of death. So it is as if He, the Exalted, said: whenever the cessation of revelation occurs, it indicates death; but death is better for you, for what you have with Allah the Exalted in the Hereafter is more excellent than what you have in this world. This, as you see, is much weaker than what precedes it.

What is evident from what they have established is that the sentence is a new (independent) sentence, and the lam in it is inceptive (ibtida'iyyah).

[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 93 (al-Duha), verse 5]

Several scholars have stated that the lam here is of the same kind in the words of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be well-pleased﴾. They said: its purpose is to emphasize the content of a sentence, and after it there is an omitted subject; that is, "And indeed you, your Lord will surely give you," and so on. It has been objected that emphasis requires attention and omission contradicts it. For this reason Ibn al-Hajib (d. 646 AH) said: the subject emphasized by the lam is not omitted, and the lam with the subject is like qad with the verb and inna with the noun. Just as the verb and the noun are not omitted and remain after their omission, so the subject is not omitted and the lam remains. Moreover, this requires an assumed element, while the original is its absence. Also, the lam serves to free the present-tense verb within its scope for the present time, as in emphasizing the content of the sentence, and here it is combined with the particle of deferment (ḥarf al-tanfis), so there is a contradiction. It has been answered that what is emphasized is the whole sentence, not the subject alone, so that its emphasis would conflict with omitting it. The statement of Ibn al-Hajib is not a proof against al-Farisi and those like him. Also, the noun may often be omitted along with it, as the grammarians have mentioned, and the verb may also be omitted after it, as in the saying of the poet:

The time of departure has drawn near, but our camels have not yet been loaded with our baggage, and it is as if (it had already happened).

Even if this is granted, al-Tibi said that a distinction may be made between inna, qad and this lam: the first two affect what follows them along with emphasis, unlike this lam, whose function is only to emphasize the content of the sentence, and this remains even if the subject is omitted. Then the analogy is an analogy with a difference. The grammarians assume many things in speech, as they assumed the subject in such phrases as: "I stood, and I strike his eye." That is for the sake of grammatical structure, not meaning, as in our present case. We do not accept that the emphatic lam serves to free the present verb for the present time as well; rather it is for mere emphasis alone, and the present sense is understood from context, since that is more suitable to emphasis. Even if we grant that it frees the verb for the present, it is possible to say that here it has become purely emphatic, by the indication of the word sawfa after it, and the intended emphasis is on the deferred element, namely the giving, not on the deferment itself. So the meaning is that the giving will certainly occur, even if delayed for a wisdom. Even if we grant that it serves both purposes and is not stripped of the present sense, it is possible to say that the future, namely the giving that is followed by contentment, is treated as though it were an actual present reality because of the certainty of its occurrence, like the statement about the verse ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. It has been said that this is very fitting in our case if we hold that the giving had already begun when the verse was revealed, according to one of its interpretations that will follow, after God wills. Some held that the first lam is the lam of oath, and so is this lam, and many affirmed this oath-function. On this view the waw is for coordination, so both promises fall within what is sworn to, and God will have sworn to four things: two negated and two affirmed. In my view this is good. It was objected that the lam of oath does not enter the present-tense verb except with the emphatic nun (al-nun al-mu'akkidah), so if it were the lam of oath it would have been said: "Surely your Lord will give you." This is not hidden, since this is one of two opinions among the grammarians. The other opinion is that what is joined to the particle of deferment is excepted, as here. In al-Mughni it is stated that the lam is obligatory and the nun is prohibited in such a case, as in the saying of the poet:

By my Lord, surely he will be recompensed for what a man has done before, whether evil or good.

Likewise when a complement separates the lam from the verb, as in: ﴿And if you die or are killed, surely to God you will be gathered﴾. Likewise when the verb is for the present, as in: "I swear not" (lā uqsimu). Sometimes both are prohibited, namely with a negated verb, as in: ﴿By God, you will not cease﴾. And sometimes both are required, as in the rest: ﴿And by God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾. On this view the objection does not stand, since what is prohibited without the nun is in the answer of the oath, not in the coordinated element that precedes it, as here. Indeed, what is tolerated in the follower is not tolerated in the followed. The lam was mentioned to emphasize the oath and to remind of it. In sum, this view is less of a stumbling-block than the previous one, and it does not require attributing to every lam with sawfa a function of making the present verb present, since none of the Arabic scholars held that the oath-lam frees the present verb for the present, as will be clear to anyone who examines their books. The apparent sense of the words of al-Fadil al-Kilanbawi is that each of the two lams is established to indicate the present. The way to reconcile this, if we assume that the lam in the verse is of oath, is that it is taken in its literal meaning, while sawfa is taken to mean the emphasis of the judgment. For this reason it took the place of one of the two nuns according to Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. He, may God have mercy on him, extended his discussion of this matter at length, and with the abundance of his excellence he brought forth what is unlikely to come from someone like him.

Isam al-Din said: "The more apparent view is that the clause ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah), that is: Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He abandoned you, while the Hereafter is better for you than the present life, and you choose it over it. Whoever is in such a condition, his Lord does not abandon him. In this there is guidance for the believers toward what is the basis of the servant's nearness to the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and a rebuke to the polytheists for their clinging to the affairs of this world and their turning away from the Hereafter. In that case the meaning of His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you﴾ is that He will surely give you the Hereafter. It is not hidden that in that case there is a complete interlocking of the sentences." End of quotation.

In this there is an objection: the entry of the lam upon the word "the Hereafter" (al-ākhira), together with its entry upon the sentence after it, and the preceding oath, makes the circumstantial reading very unlikely. Also, the meaning of mentioning it in that reading is not apparent from the verse, and the more apparent reading in your view would be that it is an apposition (badal) for "you," as is not hidden from you.

There is disagreement concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And surely...﴾ and so on. It was said: it is a noble promise encompassing what God, Mighty and Majestic, gave him in this world of perfection of soul, the knowledge of the first and the last, the manifestation of the affair and the elevation of the religion through the conquests that occurred in his time, may God bless him and grant him peace, and in the days of his successors, peace be upon him, and of other Islamic rulers, the spreading of the call and of Islam in the east and west of the earth, and what He, Majestic and Exalted, has stored up for him, peace be upon him, in the Hereafter of honors that none knows but Him, Majestic in His majesty and whose bounty is all-embracing. It was also said: it is a promise concerning what God, Glorified and Exalted, gave him in this world, such as the conquest of Makkah and other things. The majority hold that it is a promise of the Hereafter. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: it is the intercession (al-shafa'ah). Something similar was related from some of the People of the House, may God be pleased with them.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* related through the route of Harb ibn Shurayh, who said: I said to Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, upon their grandfather and upon them be prayers and peace: "Tell me about this intercession that the people of Iraq speak of: is it true?" He said: "Yes, by God. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah told me, from Ali, may God honor his face, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'I will intercede for my community until my Lord calls out: Are you pleased, O Muhammad? I will say: Yes, my Lord, I am pleased.'" Then he turned to me and said: "You people of Iraq say: the most hopeful verse in the Book of God, Exalted is He, is: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God; indeed God forgives all sins﴾." I said: "Indeed we say that." He said: "We, the People of the House, all say: the most hopeful verse in the Book of God, Exalted is He, is: ﴿And surely your Lord will give you, and you will be well-pleased﴾," and he said: "It is the intercession."

It was said: it is more general than the intercession and other things. What points to this is what al-Askari in *al-Mawa'iz*, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn al-Najjar related from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, entered upon Fatimah while she was grinding with the hand-mill, wearing a garment of camel hide. When he looked at her he said: 'O Fatimah, hasten the bitterness of this world with the bliss of the Hereafter tomorrow.' Then God, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And surely your Lord will give you, and you will be well-pleased﴾."

Abu Hayyan said: the better view is generality, covering what is in this world and the Hereafter in their various kinds, and the mentioned report, even if its authenticity be granted, does not contradict this. Indeed, the gifts of the Hereafter are far greater than the gifts of this world. Al-Hakim related it, declared it sound, and a group did likewise, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "God gave him in Paradise a thousand palaces of pearl, whose dust is musk, in each palace whatever befits him of spouses and servants."

Ibn Jarir related from him that he said: among the meaning of the verse is the contentment of Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, that no member of his household enter the Fire. Al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* related from him that he said: his contentment, may God bless him and grant him peace, is that He admit all of his community into Paradise. In the narration of al-Khatib in *Talkhis al-Mutashabih* through another route from him: "Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, will not be content while any one of his community is in the Fire." This is what his great compassion for his community, peace be upon him, requires; for he, may God bless him and grant him peace, was eager for them, kind to them, and concerned with their affairs.

Muslim related, as in *ad-Durr al-Manthur*, from Ibn Umar that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, recited God's saying concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Whoever follows me, then he is of me﴾, and His saying concerning Jesus: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾, to the end of the verse. Then he, peace be upon him, raised his hands and said: "O God, my community, my community," and he wept. God, Exalted is He, said: "O Gabriel, go to Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and say to him: Indeed We will satisfy you concerning your community, and We will not grieve you."

In repeating the name of the Lord together with its attribution to His pronoun, peace be upon him, there is also, as is not hidden, a subtle kindness toward him, may God bless him and grant him peace.

[p. 160] [p. 161]

The saying of Allah Most High, ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾, is an enumeration of the great blessings of various kinds that God Most High bestowed upon the Prophet (ﷺ) from the beginning of his life until the time of the revelation. This is so that he might find evidence in the particular, which exists, for the general, which was promised, and so that his noble heart and expansive breast would be further reassured, delighted, relieved and gladdened. For this reason the sentence is detached (fasl), and the interrogative hamza is for denying a negation, establishing the affirmation in the most eloquent manner, as if it were said: "He has indeed found you..." etc.

Regarding wajada (وَجَدَ, "to find"), according to al-Radi, it means aṣabtahu ʿalā ṣifatin (أصبتُهُ عَلى صِفَةٍ, "I came upon him in a certain state"), and by wujūd (وُجُود, "finding") is meant knowledge (ʿilm) figuratively, through the relation of necessity (ʿalāqat al-luzūm).

In al-Raghib's Mufradat (a lexicon of Qur'anic vocabulary): wujūd (finding) by the outward senses, wujūd by the inner faculties, and wujūd by the intellect. What is ascribed to God Most High of wujūd is in the sense of pure knowledge, since God Most High is exalted above being described with limbs and instruments. Some commentators have explained it here as knowledge, making its first object the pronoun and its second object yatīman (an orphan). Others have explained it as "coming upon" (muṣādafa), making it transitive to one object, with yatīman as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). You know that muṣādafa is not valid with respect to Him, Exalted is He, because it is an encounter with something that was not in His knowledge and decree, Glorified is He; therefore it is necessary to take it figuratively, meaning the attachment of His knowledge, Mighty and Majestic is He, to that matter.

Yutm (يُتْم, "orphanhood") is a child's separation from his father before reaching maturity. Iwā' (إيواء, "giving shelter") is joining one thing to another. It is said: āwā ilayhi fulānan (آوى إليه فلانًا), meaning he joined him to himself, i.e., did He not find you a child without a father, and then join you to the one who took charge of your affairs?

It is narrated that ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib sent his son ʿAbd Allah, the father of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to bring dates from Yathrib, and he died while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was still in the womb, six months after conception. When his mother gave birth to him, he was in the care of his grandfather together with his mother. She died when he (ﷺ) was six years old. When he (ﷺ) reached eight years of age, his grandfather died, and his affectionate and close paternal uncle Abu Ṭalib took charge of him in accordance with the bequest of his father ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and raised him (ﷺ) in an excellent manner.

In al-Kashshaf: his mother (ﷺ) died when he was eight years old, and his uncle took charge of him and was very attentive to his affairs until God Most High sent him as a prophet. And he saw in him (ﷺ), in his childhood, what he had not seen in any child.

It is narrated that one day he said to his brother al-ʿAbbas: "Shall I not tell you about Muhammad (ﷺ) and what I have seen of him?"

He said: "Yes."

He said: "I took him to myself, and I did not part from him for an hour of the night or the day, and I did not entrust him to anyone. I used to put him to sleep in my bed. One night I ordered him to take off his clothes and sleep with me, and I saw dislike on his face, and he disliked to oppose me. So he said: 'O uncle, turn your face away from me until I take off my clothes; I do not like that you look at my body.' I was amazed at his words and turned my gaze away until he entered the bed. When I entered the bed with him, there was a garment between me and him. By Allah, I had not put it into my bed, and he was in extreme softness and pleasant comfort, as if he had been dipped in musk. I strained to look at his body but I could not see anything. Often I would lose him from my bed, and when I rose to look for him, he would call out to me: 'Here I am, O uncle, return.' I often heard from him words that pleased me, and that was when part of the night had passed. We did not mention Allah's name over food and drink, nor did we praise Him, but he used to say at the beginning of his meal: 'In the name of Allah, the One,' and when he finished his meal he said: 'Praise be to Allah.' I was amazed at him. I never saw him tell a lie, nor laugh frivolously, nor act in the manner of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance), nor did he stop with children when they were playing. And this, by my life, is a drop from an ocean:"

In the cradle, the trace of nobility clearly indicates the happiness of his grandfather, shining with manifest proof.

Page 162

It was also said that the meaning is: did He not find you orphaned from being rejected by the wet-nurses, and then give you shelter by means of a nursing mother who showed you tenderness, by granting her, through your companionship, goodness and blessing, until she loved you and took charge of you? The first is the apparent meaning, and other things have been said, which you will learn later, if God Most High wills.

Among the strange (bidaʿ) interpretations, according to al-Zamakhshari, is that yatīman derives from the saying "a unique pearl" (durra yatīma), and the meaning is: did He not find you a unique one among Quraysh, without equal, and so give you shelter? The better reading according to this would be: did He not find you a unique one without equal in creation, whom the shell of possibility did not contain the like of, and so He gave you shelter toward Himself and placed you in the right of His choosing.

Abu al-Ash'ath read fa-āwā (فَأوى) as a triliteral verb, so it is permitted that it be from awāhu, meaning āwāhu (he gave him shelter), and that it be from awā lahu, meaning he had mercy on him. Its verbal noun is ayāwāyah, māwiyyah and māwiyah. Its realisation, according to al-Raghib, is that he returned to him with his heart. From it is his saying:

Or that I, and there is no ingratitude toward God, [...]

And His saying, ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾, is a coordination (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction) with what the preceding negative interrogative (*inkar*) implies, as has been indicated, or with the negated present verb preceded by *lam* that falls under its ruling. It is as if it were said: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? And did He not find you unaware of the sacred laws (*shara'i'*) which the intellects cannot reach by themselves, as in His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾? So He guided you to its ways (*manahij*) within what was revealed to you of the Manifest Book, and taught you what you did not know." This is, as al-Wahidi said, the view of most of the exegetes, and it is the preference of al-Zajjaj.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrated that (ﷺ) travelled to Syria with his uncle Abu Talib. One night, while he was riding a she-camel in darkness and was asleep, Iblis came to him, took hold of the camel's halter and turned it away from the road. Then Jibril, upon him be peace, came and blew upon Iblis a blast, from which he fell in Abyssinia, and he (Jibril) returned him to the caravan. So the verse contains an allusion to this, according to what has been said.

It was also said that it is an allusion to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that (ﷺ) got lost while he was young, away from his grandfather, in the mountain passes of Makkah. Abu Jahl saw him returning from his flocks and brought him back to his grandfather, who was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, supplicating Allah, exalted is He, to return Muhammad to him. It was mentioned that when he saw him, he made the camel kneel and had him ride behind him, but she refused to rise; so he had him ride in front of him, and she rose. The camel was saying: "O fool! He is the imam, so how can he stand behind the one who follows him?" And in his (ﷺ) being returned to his family by the hand of Abu Jahl, while He, glorified is He, knew of him that Abu Jahl was his Pharaoh, there is a resemblance to the return of Musa, upon him be peace, to his mother by the hand of Pharaoh.

It was also said: he (ﷺ) got lost a second time, and they searched for him but did not find him. So 'Abd al-Muttalib circled the Ka'bah seven times and supplicated Allah, exalted is He, and they heard a caller calling from the sky: "O assembly of people, do not clamour! For Muhammad has a Lord who will not forsake him nor neglect him, and Muhammad is in the valley of Tihamah, near the sumr tree." So 'Abd al-Muttalib and Waraqah ibn Nawfal set out, and suddenly the Prophet (ﷺ) was standing under a tree, playing with its branches and leaves.

It was also said: his wet-nurse Halimah lost him near the gate of Makkah, when she had weaned him, and she came with him to return him to 'Abd al-Muttalib. According to these narrations, *dallan* (ضالا, "lost") is from *dalla fi tariqihi* (ضَلَّ فِي طَرِيقِهِ), meaning when one takes a road that does not lead to one's destination. The interpretation of the verse in this sense has been considered weak, because such a thing, in comparison with what preceded, is not counted among the blessings of Allah upon one like His Prophet (ﷺ), by which He bestows favour upon him, glorified is He.

It was also said: *al-dall* is a lone tree standing in the desert with no other tree around it. The meaning would be: "Did He not find you alone, with no one with you, and so guide people to you, and not leave you solitary?"

Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: That is, He found you perplexed (*mutahayyiran*) regarding the explanation of the Book revealed to you, and so guided you to its explanation. This is close in meaning to the first view.

Some of them said: He found you unaware of the measure of your own self, and so made you aware of your great station.

It was also said: He found you lost regarding the meaning of pure love (*mahabbah*), so He gave you a cup of the drink of nearness and love, and guided you by it to the knowledge of Him, mighty and majestic.

Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: You were lost regarding My love for you in pre-eternity, so I bestowed upon you the favour of knowing Me. This is close to the previous view.

Al-Hariri said: That is, He found you wavering in the subtle meanings of love, so He guided you to them. This also is of the same kind. All of these are Sufi tendencies (*manza' sufi*).

Abu Hayyan saw in his dream that the speech is by elision of a noun (*hadhf mudaf*), and the meaning is: "And He found your people (*rahtaka*) lost, so He guided them through you." And this, as you see, is what happens in one's waking state.

[Page 163]

Allah's statement: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ follows the pattern of the verse before it. The *ʿāʾil* is the *muftaqir*, the one in need, from *āla yaʿīlu ʿaylan*, *ʿaylatan*, *ʿuyūlan* and *maʿīlan*, meaning he became poor. The meaning is: He found you without possessions and enriched you with the profit you gained from trade, during his (ﷺ) journey to Syria with Maysara, and with the wealth Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her) gave you. She was a woman of great wealth, and when he (ﷺ) married her, she gave him all of it, so that no one would say anything that would weigh heavily on his noble hearing (peace be upon him). And [he was enriched] with the wealth of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), who was also wealthy, and he brought all of it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

He (ﷺ) said: "What have you left for your dependants?" He replied: "I have left them Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ)."

It has been said: [the meaning is] by what He bestowed upon you of spoils of war. But this is objectionable, since the sura is Meccan, whereas the spoils came after the Hijra. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that He made you content and enriched your heart, for the richness of the heart is true richness. It has been said: whoever lacks contentment, wealth does not give him richness. It has also been said: He enriched you with Himself, mighty and majestic, above all else, and this richness comes through need of Him, exalted is He.

In a hadith: "O Allah, enrich me through my need of You, and do not make me poor through my independence from You."

With this in mind, some poets said:

"I am pleased with my poverty before You, and it would not please me were it not for my love of You, the poverty."

And the saying spread: "Poverty is my pride."

Poverty in it has been understood in this sense. But according to Ibn Hajar, it is false and fabricated, and more fabricated and more false is what some Sufis (*mutasawwifa*) mention: "When poverty is complete, it is Allah, exalted is He above what they say, a great exaltation." They have delved into explaining what is meant by it, in a way that does not remove its ugliness, nor even makes it sound correct.

It has been said: *ʿāʾilan* means one with dependants, from *āla yaʿūlu ʿawlan* and *ʿiyālatan*, meaning he had many dependants. Jarir's verse can carry both meanings:

"Allah has decreed in the Book an obligation
for the wayfarer and for the needy dependant."

The second meaning appears more evident. The first meaning was preferred in the verse on the basis of Ibn Mas'ud's reading, *ʿadīman* (destitute), and because he (ﷺ) did not have dependants at the beginning of his affair (ﷺ). Al-Yamani read *ʿayyilan*, like *sayyidan*, with the letter yāʾ doubled and kasra.

Isam al-Din mentioned regarding these verses that it is possible that by the orphan is meant one who lacks a teacher, for fathers are three: the one who teaches you, the one who marries you, and the one who begets you. This fits interpreting "going astray" as going astray from knowledge, and interpreting "dependants" (in the explanation of *ʿāʾilan* as "with dependants") as the dependants of the community, who seek from him knowledge of the interests of the religion while he himself needs knowledge; so Allah enriched him through the revelation sent to him (ﷺ). But what is wrong with this is not hidden.

The object is omitted in the three verbs, since the meaning is evident and in keeping with the *fawāṣil* (verse-endings). It has been said that this is to indicate the vastness of generosity, and the intended meaning is: He sheltered you, sheltered [others] for you and through you; guided you, [guided others] for you and through you; enriched you, [enriched others] for you and through you. But the apparent particle *fa-* with these verbs rejects this.

The Imam (al-Razi) extended the discussion on these verses and included in them both the worthless and the valuable. Were it not for fear of tedium, we would have mentioned what is in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 93, verse 9:

﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him.﴾ That is, do not demean him, as Ibn Sallam (Ibn Sallam) said. Close to this is the saying of Mujahid: "Do not belittle him." Sufyan said:

"Do not wrong him by squandering his wealth." In the same sense it has been said: "Do not overpower him in respect of his wealth." Perhaps the restriction is to take account of what usually happens. The preferable reading is to take qahr (overpowering) as both domination and demeaning, two faults. What is intended is dominance through that which causes harm, or the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings, according to the view that permits this. In al-Raghib's Mufradat (Mufradat al-Raghib al-Isfahani): "Qahr is overpowering and demeaning together, and it is used for each of the two." Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi and Ibrahim al-Taymi read: «فَلا تَكْهَرْ» with a kaf instead of a qaf. Its meaning, according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): "fa-la taqhar" (so do not overpower). In Tahdhib al-Azhari (Tahdhib al-Lugha by al-Azhari): "al-kahr is al-qahr (overpowering), al-kahr is frowning of the face, and al-kahr is reviling." Some chose the middle of these senses here, so the meaning is: "do not frown in his face," and this is a prohibition of reviling and overpowering, by way of a stronger implication (min bab al-awla), as you have heard its meaning. In any case, the verse indicates concern for the affairs of the orphan.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, traced back to the Prophet (marfu'): "Whoever wipes the head of an orphan, for every hair over which his hand passes there will be a light for him on the Day of Resurrection."

It is also related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, likewise traced back to the Prophet: "Indeed, when an orphan weeps, the Throne of the Merciful shakes at his weeping. Allah, exalted is He, says to His angels: 'O My angels, who made this orphan weep, whose father has been buried in the dust?' The angels say: 'You know best.' Allah, exalted is He, says: 'O My angels, I call you to witness that upon Me, for whoever stills him and pleases him, is that I shall please him on the Day of Resurrection.'"

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to wipe the head of an orphan whenever he saw one and give him something. Nothing authentic has been transmitted regarding the manner of wiping, and the report from Ibn Abbas on this matter has been subject to what has been said about it.

It is also related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "I and the one who sponsors an orphan are like these two, if he fears Allah, exalted is He," and he pointed with the index finger and the middle finger. And other reports besides these.

[Page 164]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 93, verse 10:

﴿And as for the one who asks, do not repel him.﴾ That is: do not drive him away; rather, show him kindness with something, or turn him away with a good word. According to a group [of scholars], what is meant by "the one who asks" is the beggar (al-mustajdi), the one who seeks something of the world. The verse also indicates the importance of attending to his situation.

And Ibrahim ibn Adham said: "Excellent are the people who ask; they carry our provision to the Hereafter."

And Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "The one who asks, seeking the Hereafter, comes to the door of one of you and says: 'Will you send your family something?'"

The hadith spread: "The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on a horse."

Imam Ahmad said about it, as in Tamyiz al-Tayyib min al-Khabith: "It has no basis." Abu Dawud narrated it from al-Husayn ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a mawquf (a report ending at a Companion), and he remained silent about it. Al-Iraqi said: "Its chain is good," and others followed him. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "It is not strong." Many relied on what Imam Ahmad said. Its meaning admits of two possibilities, each of which indicates concern for the matter of the one who asks.

It is also narrated through various routes from Aisha and others: "Had the one who asks been truthful, no one who turned him away would have prospered." This too, according to Ibn al-Madini, "has no basis," and Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "All its chains are not strong." Yes, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir narrated from Abu Umama, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something close to it, which is: "Were it not that the needy lie, no one who turned them away would have prospered."

I have not come across anyone who criticized this. Then, the prohibition of "repelling" (al-nahr), as they have said, applies when he does not press his request; but if he presses and gentle refusal does not work, then there is no harm in rebuking him. Abu al-Darda', al-Hasan, Sufyan and others said: the "one who asks" here means the one who asks about knowledge and religion, not the one who asks for wealth. Perhaps the prohibition against rebuking him, on the first view, is understood a fortiori, and what supports this priority is that there is no threat for refusing to give to the beggar to one who has what he asks for, unlike refusing to answer the questioner about knowledge when one knows it. In the hadith: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it will be bridled with a bridle of fire." What has been said, that the apparent meaning is the second of the two views, will come, Allah willing, later on.

﴿And as for the favour of your Lord, proclaim it.﴾ Speaking of it is indeed gratitude for it, as Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said.

Al-Bukhari in al-Adab (*al-Adab al-Mufrad*), Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it hasan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Hibban, al-Bayhaqi and al-Diya narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever is given a gift and finds [the means], let him repay it; if he does not find [the means], let him praise it, for whoever praises it has thanked it, and whoever conceals it has denied it. And whoever adorns himself with what he has not been given is like one who wears two garments of falsehood."

For this reason some of the early scholars (*salaf*) recommended speaking of the good one has done, provided one does not intend showing off (*riya'*) or boasting and wishes that others follow his example. Indeed, some of the Family of the Prophet, may Allah be pleased with them, understood the verse in this sense.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Miqsam, who said: "I met al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with both of them and with their father, and I said: 'Tell me about the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And as for the favour of your Lord, proclaim it.﴾' He said: 'The believing man does a righteous deed and informs his household of it.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said regarding it: "When you attain some good, speak of it to your brothers."

The apparent meaning of "the favour" is the various kinds of blessings which Allah bestowed upon His Prophet (ﷺ), of which the aforementioned are part.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Mujahid that it is to be interpreted as prophethood, and they also transmitted from him an interpretation of it as the Qur'an. Muhammad ibn Ishaq agreed with him on the first, and al-Kalbi on the second. On both interpretations, "proclaiming" means conveying (*al-tabligh*). It is not hidden that both interpretations are not well suited to what precedes. These three clauses are arranged in correspondence with what came before, so it has been said that this is *al-laff wa al-nashr al-mushawwash* (a scrambled correspondence, in which the referents are listed and then matched without regard to order). The sense is: you were an orphan, lost and needy, and He sheltered you, guided you and enriched you. Whatever the case, do not forget Allah's favour upon you in these three matters, and follow the example of Allah, the Exalted, by showing tenderness to the orphan and compassion to the one who asks, for you have tasted orphanhood and poverty.

The Exalted's words ﴿And as for the favour of your Lord﴾, etc., correspond to His words: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾, because it is general and comprehensive, including His guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) from error through teaching the laws and other blessings. The verse does not observe the order, by giving precedence to the rights of the servants over His right, may He be exalted, for He, glorified and exalted, is free of need from the worlds. It has also been said that this is for the sake of putting *al-takhliya* (clearing away, i.e. removal of what is undesirable) before *al-tahliya* (adornment, i.e. bestowal of what is desirable), or for progression (*al-taraqqi*), or for the sake of the rhyme endings (*al-fawasil*), but all of these have been criticised. Al-Taybi said: "The apparent meaning is that 'the one who asks' refers to the seeker of knowledge, not the beggar. In that case there is no objection to the detail following the order, so that it is said: He, the Exalted, mentioned his (ﷺ) circumstances in accordance with the external order, by taking His guidance of him (ﷺ) to include His granting him success in sound reflection in his youth; he (ﷺ) was indeed granted success in this, and for this reason he (ﷺ) never worshipped an idol. Or His enriching him may refer to what came after the mission (*al-ba'tha*). Then He, glorified be He, expounded on that order: the non-oppression of the orphan corresponds to His sheltering him (ﷺ) in his orphanhood; the non-rebuking of the one who asks, that is the seeker of knowledge and the one learning from him, corresponds to His guidance of him; and proclaiming the favour corresponds to the enrichment, although the favour includes him and others alike."

He, glorified be He, chose ﴿fa-haddith﴾ (then proclaim) over ﴿fa-khabbir﴾ (then inform). It has been said: this is so that mention of the favour bestowed upon him (ﷺ) becomes a discourse he does not forget and which he recalls from time to time. And Allah knows best.

It is recommended to say *takbir* (the phrase Allahu akbar) at the end of this noble surah, and likewise after it up to the end of the Mighty Qur'an. Al-Hakim, who graded it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated through Abu al-Hasan al-Bazzi, the reciter, who said: "I heard Ikrimah ibn Sulayman say: 'I recited to Isma'il ibn Qusantin, and when I reached ﴿By the morning brightness﴾ he said: "Say takbir at the end of every surah until you finish." For I recited to Abd Allah ibn Kathir, and when I reached ﴿By the morning brightness﴾ he said: "Say takbir until you finish." Abd Allah ibn Kathir informed me that he had recited to Mujahid, and he commanded him to do so, and informed him that Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, commanded him to do so, and informed him that Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, commanded him to do so, and informed him that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded him to do so.'" This was from him (ﷺ) an expression of joy at the descent of revelation after its delay and slowness, to the extent that what was said was said. This is the practice of the people today, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
